players.product: Turnkey HPC data-center campuses leased to hyperscalers (Barber Lake, Black Pearl, Stingray - Texas) - ex-Bitcoin-mining, now 'Cipher Digital'

quarterly_data.quarter: Cipher Digital KBW Virtual AI Summit 2026 (10-06-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Colchis (CFO Greg Mumford): Colchis received conditional approval in base load - 'we have been approved conditionally for 1 gigawatt in the first batch'; after an audit coming up in December, 'we are hoping and expecting to be firmly approved for that gigawatt'. He called it 'a marquee asset' that is very interesting to the tenants Cipher is speaking with. On the TCEQ and the audit process, he believes regulation will affect timing rather than erode fundamental demand and may slow execution, more in some states than others; sites with approvals or outside these processes should be more valuable to tenants, and Cipher has some sites outside the audit with ongoing discussions 'in a pretty robust way'. 'Time to power and scarcity still drive most decision-making that we are seeing on the leasing front.'
quarterly_data.figure: Colchis conditionally approved for 1 gigawatt in the first batch; audit in December

quarterly_data.quarter: Cipher Digital KBW Virtual AI Summit 2026 (10-06-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Leasing demand and terms (CFO Greg Mumford): the view that demand is collapsing is 'overdone' - 'I still think scarce power is the constraint and demand is not changing from what we can see.' He called the Barber Lake commitment (an AI lab leasing the facility for 10 years after Fluidstack's term) 'the best proof point that we have in the market to date' of terminal value in these sites. Lease terms keep improving: leases that started as modified gross leases for 10 years now see '20-year leases triple net as kind of the standard', and since the Fluidstack lease was signed at the end of the summer in 2025 the discussion has moved to 20 years as 'the base starting point'. The pool of top-quality prospective tenants has grown beyond the top hyperscalers to include 'some of the chip developers' and other parties with great credit ratings. Lease levers beyond yield: SLAs with delivery penalties, termination clauses that are 'becoming more favorable to developers', and in some of Cipher's leases a pre-agreed split of costs between Cipher and a tenant (risk transference). Citing a quiet period, he did not discuss demand at the 2027 sites (Ulysses, Reveille, Odessa).
quarterly_data.figure: standard lease moved from 10-year modified gross to 20-year triple net

quarterly_data.quarter: Cipher Digital KBW Virtual AI Summit 2026 (10-06-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Behind-the-meter generation (CFO Greg Mumford): Cipher has started building the lateral gas pipelines to its sites and is 'working on various agreements that would actually transport the gas through the pipeline to our site'; it has 'very strong demand from tenants' to build a data center with behind-the-meter generation. The structuring and deal-making is 'quite challenging': many interested parties, and 'it's challenging to get access to generation equipment on a timeframe that works for the tenant'. 'Until you have it signed up, you don't have a deal yet.' These deals have a different risk profile from front-of-the-meter deals and Cipher is structuring them to be compensated for it.

quarterly_data.quarter: Cipher Digital KBW Virtual AI Summit 2026 (10-06-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Build cost and operating model (CFO Greg Mumford): 'Spec drives dollars per megawatt' - Cipher builds to each tenant's specification (redundancy, backup generators, evaporative or liquid cooling), giving a wide range of dollars per megawatt; its project budget covers everything from acquiring the site to handing over the keys and delivering down to the racks for a triple-net site, including land, permitting, soft costs, engineering and a development fee to Cipher. Inflation: the price of transformers 'is probably higher than it was 2 years ago', and deals are underwritten for it. Cipher has greenfield-sourced all of its sites to date ('in the double digit of energy assets'), keeps its EPCM function (procurement, engineering, construction management) in-house, sees potential opportunities to buy powered land that still needs to be matured through interconnection, and has not really started looking at buying stabilized assets. Recycling capital - through refinancings or monetizing a portion of an asset or a whole asset - is 'a critical piece of this business model'.
